label: E2
title: Chemical energy, combustion, and the bomb calorimeter

blocks.html: Checked against the sources as they stood on 2026-09-23.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Combustion is burning: a substance combines vigorously with oxygen.

A bomb calorimeter operates at constant volume and is used for reactions that release large amounts of energy and produce gases, which is what combustion does. It is a strong steel container, the bomb, which holds the sample and is itself submerged in water. The bomb is filled with oxygen at high pressure and a small electrical spark ignites the sample. The energy produced is taken up by the steel bomb and the water around it, and a thermometer records the rise.

A substance whose energy is already known is burned in it, and the rise that produces is measured. The known energy divided by that rise is the calorimeter’s energy equivalent, in joules for each degree. Afterwards any rise measured in that calorimeter, multiplied by that same energy equivalent, gives the energy the reaction released.

What that measures is the total combustible energy content of the food, also called its theoretical maximum energy content. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations calls this the ingested energy, or the gross energy.

Not all of it is available to a person. Incomplete digestion in the small intestine, sometimes with fermentation of unabsorbed carbohydrate in the colon, loses energy as faecal energy and as gaseous energy in combustible gases. Some of the energy that is absorbed is then lost as urinary energy, mainly as nitrogenous waste compounds from incomplete breakdown of protein. A small amount is lost from the body surface. What remains after those losses is metabolizable energy.

Below that the Organization’s 2003 report carries one further step, net metabolizable energy. It takes off the energy the body itself spends on digesting the food and on handling what is absorbed. The report’s cascade has no step called digestible energy. The phrase is not in chapter 3, where the report sets out the cascade, or in chapter 4.

The energy figure on a food label is not a burning measurement. It is derived using the Atwater system, which uses the average caloric content of protein, carbohydrate and fat. Those averages are the Atwater general factors. There is one value for each of the three, used regardless of the food it is found in. They are based on the heats of combustion of protein, fat and carbohydrate, corrected for losses in digestion, absorption and urinary excretion of urea.

The three values are 17 kilojoules for each gram of protein, 37 for each gram of fat and 17 for each gram of carbohydrate. In kilocalories for each gram the same three values are 4.0, 9.0 and 4.0.

One thing the general system does not do is take fibre out. Some labelling systems do discount fibre, as OpenStax Chemistry describes. Atwater’s general system does not. The Indian labelling regulations give dietary fibre its own factor, 2 kilocalories a gram.

To work out the energy content of a food, the quantities of carbohydrate, protein and fat are each multiplied by the factor for that one, and the products are added.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
You cannot weigh energy. What you can do is burn the food and watch a thermometer.

The machine for it is called a bomb calorimeter. The name is unhelpful and the thing is straightforward. It is a thick steel pot, sealed, sitting in a tank of water. You put a weighed scrap of dried food inside, fill the pot with oxygen, seal it, and set it off with an electric spark. The food burns completely. The warmth spreads into the steel and the water. A thermometer in the water reads higher than it did before.

Nothing about a temperature rise tells you how many joules it took. That depends on the machine: how much steel, how much water, how it is built.

You burn something whose energy you already know. You watch how far the thermometer goes up. Then you divide.

the energy equivalent = the known energy, divided by the rise it caused

Call it the calorimeter’s energy equivalent. Doing this is called calibrating the machine, and it is done again before each set of measurements rather than once when the machine is bought.

After that the work is one multiplication.

the energy released = the rise, times the energy equivalent

Burn a known thing to get the constant, then burn the unknown thing and multiply.

What you have measured is all the energy the food will give up when it is burnt to nothing. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations calls it the gross energy. It is the most the food could ever supply.

A person is not a furnace.

Some food is not digested and absorbed at all, and leaves in the faeces, carrying its energy with it. Some unabsorbed carbohydrate is fermented in the large intestine and leaves as gas, which also carries energy. Some of what is absorbed leaves in the urine, mostly as the waste left when protein is broken down and not finished off. And a small amount is lost from the body surface.

What is left after those losses has a name. It is called metabolizable energy, spelt with a z in the report that names it.

So the cascade is gross energy, then metabolizable energy. Below that the report carries one more step, called net metabolizable energy. It takes off the energy the body itself spends on digesting the food and handling it. The report’s cascade has no step called digestible energy. The phrase is not in chapter 3, where the report sets out the cascade, or in chapter 4. You may hear somebody put one in the middle and say the report has it. If they do, they have not read that chapter.

The number on a packet was almost certainly never measured by burning anything. It was calculated.

The fixed figures are called the Atwater general factors.

what it is kilojoules a gram kilocalories a gram
protein 17 4.0
fat 37 9.0
carbohydrate 17 4.0

Those factors already have the losses taken out of them. They were built from burning measurements and then corrected for what is lost in digestion, in absorption and in the urine.

So the figure on the packet is an estimate of metabolizable energy for an average, arrived at by arithmetic on three weights. It is a good estimate and it is not a measurement of that packet.

Burning tells you what is in the food. The factors tell you what an average person would get out of it. Neither one tells you anything about the person in front of you.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Open OpenStax Chemistry 2e, section 5.2, Calorimetry, at https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/5-2-calorimetry. Open your browser’s find box and search inside the page for the word bomb.

The sample is placed in the bomb, which is then filled with oxygen at high pressure. A small electrical spark is used to ignite the sample.

Now search the same page for the word calibration, because that is the word this whole section turns on.

The calibration is generally performed each time before the calorimeter is used to gather research data.

Each time. Not once when the machine arrives.

How many joules one degree is worth depends on this machine.

Every figure in this calorimeter example is made up.

The known sample releases 26,400 joules. The thermometer goes up by 2.2 degrees Celsius, which is the ordinary degree marked on a kitchen thermometer.

Divide the energy by the rise.

26,400 divided by 2.2 = 12,000

That is the calorimeter’s energy equivalent, and it is the only thing you needed.

A dried pellet of food weighing 1.50 grams goes in, and the thermometer goes up by 1.85 degrees.

12,000 times 1.85 = 22,200

Put it in kilojoules, because nobody quotes food in joules.

22,200 divided by 1,000 = 22.2

Now for each gram, since the pellet weighed 1.50 grams.

22.2 divided by 1.50 = 14.8

Turn it into the unit food is quoted in, using the 4.184 from the section on energy units.

14.8 divided by 4.184 = 3.5373

About 3.5 kilocalories in each gram.

The question nobody asks is what it is a number about.

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations published a report on this in 2003. Open chapter 3 of it at https://www.fao.org/4/y5022e/y5022e04.htm.

Almost everybody who has met this once remembers three steps: gross energy, then digestible energy, then metabolisable energy. Search the page for digestible energy.

The phrase is not in the chapter.

Search for gross energy instead.

Food that is ingested contains energy - the maximum amount being reflected in the heat that is measured after complete combustion to carbon dioxide (CO2) and water in a bomb calorimeter. This energy is referred to as ingested energy (IE) or gross energy (GE).

That is your burning measurement, named.

The energy that remains after accounting for the important losses is known as “metabolizable energy” (ME) (see Figure 3.1).

Now read one paragraph further. There is a third step, and it is not the one you went looking for. Some energy is spent on digesting the food and handling it afterwards, and some is lost to microbes. Take those off metabolizable energy and the report names what is left.

…the result is an expression of the energy content of food, which is referred to as net metabolizable energy (NME).

So the report’s cascade runs gross energy, then metabolizable energy, then net metabolizable energy. There is no digestible-energy step in it. The phrase is not in chapter 3, and it is not in chapter 4 either.

Search the same chapter for Atwater.

The energy values are 17 kJ/g (4.0 kcal/g) for protein, 37 kJ/g (9.0 kcal/g) for fat and 17 kJ/g (4.0 kcal/g) for carbohydrates.

Open the National Food Security Act, 2013 at https://indiacode.gov.in/handle/123456789/496105 and go to Schedule II. Find the row for upper primary classes. The hot cooked meal is set at 700 in the energy column, and at 20 grams in the protein column.

Work out how much of that 700 the protein standard accounts for.

20 times 4.0 = 80

As a share of the meal, divide the part by the whole.

80 divided by 700 = 0.1142857143

Keep every figure for now. Multiply by a hundred to turn the proportion into a percentage.

0.1142857143 times 100 = 11.42857143

Round once, at the end: 11.4. About eleven per cent. So the Act fixes an energy figure and a protein figure, and the protein figure accounts for roughly a ninth of the energy. The other eight ninths have to come from fat and carbohydrate, and Schedule II sets no figure for either of them.

Now do the same sum in kilojoules and watch something strange happen. The factor for protein in kilojoules is 17.

20 times 17 = 340

And the 700 kilocalories, in kilojoules:

700 times 4.184 = 2,928.8

340 divided by 2,928.8 = 0.1160885004

0.1160885004 times 100 = 11.60885004

Round once, at the end: 11.6. Eleven point six per cent this time, against eleven point four the other way.

The report’s kilojoule column and its kilocalorie column were each rounded on their own, and they are not exact conversions of one another. A footnote on the same page gives protein’s precise value as 16.7 kilojoules a gram, and that one does convert properly.

16.7 divided by 4.184 = 3.991

The 17 is the rounded figure, and rounding it is what moved your answer in the third digit.

You do not have a measurement of any meal. Schedule II says what a meal must meet, not what any meal contained.

You do not have what reaches a child either, even if a meal met the standard exactly.

This book does not carry either number, and you should not supply one from memory.

Every time somebody hands you a food-energy figure, ask three questions in order. Was it burnt or was it calculated. Is it the gross figure or the metabolizable one. And is it a standard somebody set, or a measurement somebody took.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Every figure in the calorimeter example is made up. Only the 4.184, the Atwater factors and the two Schedule II figures come from a source.

The energy equivalent belongs to one calorimeter on one day. Carry it to another machine and every answer it gives is wrong, and wrong silently, because the arithmetic still works.

The method needs the sample to burn completely. Nothing in the arithmetic will tell you it happened.

The Atwater factors are averages over foods. So the method cannot tell apart two foods with the same grams of protein, fat and carbohydrate.

The two printed columns pair up for protein and for carbohydrate. They do not pair up for fat. The footnote that gave protein’s 16.7 gives fat’s precise value as 37.4 kilojoules a gram, and the report prints 9.0 kilocalories beside it. Try the conversion both ways round.

37.4 divided by 4.184 = 8.9388
9.0 times 4.184 = 37.656

Read each column as its own set of numbers and do not work one out from the other.

The eleven per cent figure is a share of two numbers the Act sets, not a share of anything a child ate.

None of the arithmetic here says anything about a person. It gives you what is in a food and what an average person would get out of it. What one person absorbs, what they spend, and what any change in their body would be made of are three separate questions. This book answers none of them.

points.html: A bomb calorimeter figure is the food’s total combustible energy. It is not the energy a person gets. So never quote a burning figure as what somebody received.

The report’s cascade has no digestible-energy step. It runs from gross or ingested energy to metabolizable energy. The losses named are faecal, gaseous, urinary and surface. A third step sits below, net metabolizable energy. So do not object to a three-step reading of this report. Object to the word digestible when it is credited to this cascade. Name the step that was made up.
A temperature rise is not an energy until the machine that produced it has been calibrated. The calibration is repeated before each set of runs, not done once.

The Atwater general factors are the numbers behind nearly every food-energy figure you will ever be handed. They are 17 kilojoules, or 4.0 kilocalories, for each gram of protein. For fat they are 37 or 9.0, and for carbohydrate 17 or 4.0. Knowing them means you can recompute any label yourself instead of trusting it.
Those factors use one value for each of protein, fat and carbohydrate, whatever the food. It cannot show that one food is taken up better than another.

The energy declared on an Indian packet is worked out from the grams, not measured by burning anything. So two packets showing the same figure have been through the same arithmetic, not the same measurement.
When a journalist gives you a food-energy figure, the useful sentence is about what it describes. Give them that line before you argue about the number itself.

Teach the calibration before the formula. A trainee who has seen a known burn turned into a constant will never again treat a thermometer reading as an energy. They will also carry the question to every instrument they meet afterwards: what was this measured against.

blocks.prompt:
Without looking back, write down the two steps that turn a bomb calorimeter reading into an energy, in order, and say what each step needs.

Then write down the cascade the Food and Agriculture Organization’s report gives for what happens to a food’s energy in a person, naming the losses.
blocks.answer:
The two steps of the instrument.

First, calibrate. Burn something whose energy is already known and measure the rise it produces. Divide the known energy by that rise. What you get is the calorimeter’s energy equivalent, in joules for each degree, and it belongs to that one machine.

Second, measure. Burn the unknown sample, measure its rise, and multiply the rise by that same energy equivalent. That is the energy released.

What each step needs: the first needs a substance of known energy, the second needs nothing except the constant from the first.

The cascade. The food that is eaten holds its gross energy, also called ingested energy, which is what a bomb calorimeter measures. Then come the losses.

Energy is lost in the faeces, from food that is not digested and absorbed. Energy is lost as gas, from unabsorbed carbohydrate fermented in the colon. Energy is lost in the urine, mostly as nitrogenous waste from protein that was not fully broken down. A small amount is lost from the body surface. What remains is metabolizable energy.

Below that the report carries one more step, net metabolizable energy. It takes off the energy the body itself spends on digesting the food and handling it.

One thing to check in your own answer. Did you write a digestible-energy step in the middle? It is not in the report’s cascade, and the habit of putting it there is exactly what this section is for.

blocks.prompt:
A supplement company’s sheet says this. The company and the sheet are made up for this exercise. Read it twice before you answer.

Independent laboratory testing by bomb calorimetry confirms that each serving delivers 480 kilocalories of energy to the body. The measurement was made by burning, so it is more accurate than the numbers worked out on paper for ordinary packets.

Say what is wrong. Then say what you would ask for.
blocks.answer:
There are three claims here and they fail in three different ways.

The first is the phrase delivers to the body. A bomb calorimeter burns the sample to nothing in pure oxygen. What it measures is the gross energy, which is the most the food could ever supply. It cannot measure what reaches a person, because the faecal, gaseous and urinary losses happen in a person and not in a steel pot.

The second is the comparison with a label figure. A calculated label figure uses the Atwater factors, and those factors already have average losses taken out of them. So the calculated figure is an estimate of metabolizable energy and the burning figure is gross energy. They are numbers about different things. The burning figure will be the larger of the two, and being larger is not being more accurate.

The third is the word confirms, doing work that one measurement cannot do. A single run in one calorimeter rests entirely on that machine’s calibration constant on that day.

What to ask for. The calibration record for the machine, with the date and the substance of known energy that was burnt. The number of runs and the spread across them. Whether the fuse wire was weighed before and after, which is how anyone knows the sample burnt completely. And the composition of the serving in grams, so you can do the Atwater sum yourself and see how far the two figures sit apart.

And say the main point in one line, because it is the one that gets waved through. Burning a food tells you what is in the food. It does not tell you what the food gives to a person, and no amount of care with the instrument will make it do so.

blocks.prompt:
A health secretary has one page. They have been handed a proposal about a school meal scheme. It argues the scheme is meeting its target, because the menu adds up to the energy figure in the standard.

Write what you would put on the page. Answer first, no methods section.
blocks.answer:
Answer first, one page, no methods.

The proposal has shown that the menu is designed to meet the standard. It has not shown that the scheme is meeting it. Those are two different claims and only the first has evidence behind it.

Three gaps, in the order they matter.

The first is between the menu and the plate. A menu is an intention. What a child receives depends on what was cooked, how much of it was served, and whether it was eaten. None of that is in an arithmetic total.

The second is between the plate and the child. The figure in the standard is a food-energy figure. Some of the energy in any food is lost in the faeces, some as gas, and some in the urine. So the energy available to a child is always less than the energy in the food. The proposal’s total is the upper figure.

The third is between the child’s intake and any outcome anyone cares about. What a child spends is not in this arithmetic at all, and nothing in a menu total establishes a result.

What would close the gaps, in order of cost. Weighed portions on a sample of days at a sample of schools, which turns the menu into a measurement. Plate waste on the same days, which turns what was served into what was eaten. Both are ordinary field measurements and neither needs a laboratory.

What not to spend money on: burning food samples in a calorimeter. It would answer, very precisely, the question the proposal has already answered. It would say nothing about the two that are open.

One line for the meeting. The menu arithmetic is right. It is arithmetic about a plan, and the question in front of you is about a plate.

blocks.prompt:
One kilocalorie is 4.184 kilojoules.

Turn 2,092 kilojoules into kilocalories.
blocks.answer:
Kilojoules to kilocalories means dividing, because a kilocalorie is the bigger unit and there will be fewer of them.

2,092 divided by 4.184 = 500

Five hundred kilocalories.

Check the direction before you move on. The answer came out smaller than the number you started with, and that is right. One kilocalorie is worth more than four kilojoules. So any amount of energy is a smaller number when it is counted in kilocalories.

blocks.prompt:
A calorimeter’s energy equivalent is 9,500 joules for each degree.

In one run the thermometer rises by 3.4 degrees. Work out the energy released, first in joules and then in kilojoules. The figures in this problem are made up.
blocks.answer:
The energy equivalent is a number of joules for each degree, so multiply it by the number of degrees.

9,500 times 3.4 = 32,300

Thirty-two thousand three hundred joules.

A kilojoule is a thousand joules, so divide.

32,300 divided by 1,000 = 32.3

Thirty-two point three kilojoules.

blocks.prompt:
A sample whose energy is known to be 44,000 joules is burned in a calorimeter. The thermometer rises by 4.00 degrees.

Work out how many joules one degree is worth in that calorimeter. The figures in this problem are made up.
blocks.answer:
This is the calibration, and it runs the other way from the last problem. There you had the constant and wanted the energy. Here you have the energy and want the constant.

Divide the known energy by the rise it produced.

44,000 divided by 4.00 = 11,000

Eleven thousand joules for each degree.

Check the unit, because it is what tells you the answer is the right kind of thing.

joules, divided by degrees
= joules per degree

That number now belongs to this calorimeter and to no other.

blocks.prompt:
A sample holds 12 grams of protein, 8 grams of fat and 40 grams of carbohydrate.

Using 4.0 for each gram of protein, 9.0 for each gram of fat and 4.0 for each gram of carbohydrate, work out the total.
blocks.answer:
Take each of the three on its own, then add.

12 times 4.0 = 48

8 times 9.0 = 72

40 times 4.0 = 160

Now add the three.

48 plus 72 plus 160 = 280

Two hundred and eighty.

Look at the three parts before you leave it. The fat is a fifth of the weight of the carbohydrate. It gives almost half as much energy. That is what a factor of nine does against a factor of four.

blocks.prompt:
Food and Nutrition Paper 77 is a report on food energy. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations published it in 2003.

It gives the Atwater general factor for protein twice over. Once as 17 kilojoules for each gram, and once as 4.0 kilocalories for each gram. A footnote on the same page gives the precise figure as 16.7 kilojoules a gram.

Turn both of those kilojoule figures into kilocalories a gram. One kilocalorie is 4.184 kilojoules. Then say which of the two the report’s 4.0 was rounded from.
blocks.answer:
Take the rounded figure first.

17 divided by 4.184 = 4.063

Four point zero six kilocalories a gram.

Now the precise figure from the footnote.

16.7 divided by 4.184 = 3.991

Three point nine nine kilocalories a gram.

Which one the 4.0 came from: the second. Three point nine nine rounds to four point zero. Four point zero six does not, at least not without throwing away a digit you were given.

So the report’s two columns are not exact conversions of one another. They were set down separately, and for protein the precise kilojoule figure does round to the printed kilocalorie one. Convert the rounded 17 instead and you land near the printed figure, not on it.

What to do about it in practice. Use whichever unit the source you are quoting used, and convert only when you have to. Every conversion of a rounded figure moves the answer. A move of a few parts in a thousand is enough to make two people think one of them has slipped.

blocks.prompt:
A laboratory calibrates a bomb calorimeter by burning a sample whose energy is known to be 52,500 joules. The thermometer rises by 3.50 degrees Celsius.

It then burns a 2.00 gram dried pellet of a food, and the thermometer rises by 2.80 degrees Celsius.

Work out the energy the food released, in kilojoules, and then the energy for each gram of food. Write the unit on every line. Every figure in this problem is made up; no real calorimeter and no real food is being described.
blocks.answer:
Calibrate first. Known energy divided by the rise it caused.

52,500 divided by 3.50 = 15,000

Fifteen thousand joules for each degree, for this calorimeter.

Now the food. Rise times the energy equivalent.

15,000 times 2.80 = 42,000

Forty-two thousand joules. Into kilojoules.

42,000 divided by 1,000 = 42

Forty-two kilojoules from the whole pellet. The pellet weighed 2.00 grams, so divide.

42 divided by 2.00 = 21

Twenty-one kilojoules in each gram of that food.

Keep the label as well as the unit. This is twenty-one kilojoules of gross energy for each gram of the dried food. Dried is not the same as eaten, because the water was taken out. And gross energy is not the same as what a person would get from it.

blocks.prompt:
Schedule II of the National Food Security Act, 2013 sets standards for a hot cooked meal. For lower primary classes it sets 450 in the energy column and 12 grams in the protein column. The energy column is headed Calories, with Kcal in brackets.

The Atwater general factor for protein is 4.0 kilocalories for each gram. Work out how many of those 450 kilocalories the protein standard accounts for. Then work out what share of the meal that is, as a percentage.
blocks.answer:
The protein first. Grams times the factor for protein.

12 times 4.0 = 48

Forty-eight kilocalories from the protein standard.

Now the share. Divide the part by the whole, which here is the energy standard for the same meal.

48 divided by 450 = 0.1066666667

Keep every figure for now. Turn the proportion into a percentage by multiplying by a hundred.

0.1066666667 times 100 = 10.66666667

Round once, at the end: 10.7. About ten point seven per cent.

Read the unit on the 450 before you leave this. The column is headed Calories with Kcal in brackets, so the figure is kilocalories. Taken as plain calories it would be a meal of 450 calories. In joules that is this.

450 times 4.184 = 1,882.8

That is under two kilojoules, and no meal is that.

And read what the answer is about. It is the share of the Act’s energy standard that the Act’s protein standard accounts for. It is not the protein share of any meal a child ate.

blocks.prompt:
Two laboratories are given the same dried food and asked for its energy for each gram.

The first burns it. Its calorimeter is worth 8,000 joules for each degree, and a 1.25 gram sample makes the thermometer rise by 2.50 degrees.

The second does not burn anything. It measures the composition instead. In each gram it finds 0.10 grams of protein, 0.05 grams of fat and 0.70 grams of carbohydrate. The rest is water and minerals. It uses the Atwater general factors of 4.0, 9.0 and 4.0 kilocalories a gram.

Work out both answers in kilocalories for each gram. Say which is larger, by how much, and why you would have expected that before doing the arithmetic. All the figures are made up for this problem.
blocks.answer:
The first laboratory. Rise times the energy equivalent.

8,000 times 2.50 = 20,000

20,000 divided by 1,000 = 20

Twenty kilojoules from a 1.25 gram sample.

20 divided by 1.25 = 16

Sixteen kilojoules for each gram. Into kilocalories.

16 divided by 4.184 = 3.824

Three point eight two kilocalories a gram.

The second laboratory. Each component times its own factor, then add.

0.10 times 4.0 = 0.4

0.05 times 9.0 = 0.45

0.70 times 4.0 = 2.8

0.4 plus 0.45 plus 2.8 = 3.65

Three point six five kilocalories a gram.

The difference:

3.824 minus 3.65 = 0.174

The burning answer is the larger, by about 0.17 kilocalories a gram.

Why that was the expected direction. The calorimeter measures gross energy: everything the food gives up when it is burnt to nothing. The Atwater factors were built from burning measurements and then corrected for what is lost in digestion, in absorption and in the urine. So the factors are already a step down the cascade. A figure worked out from them should come out below a burning figure for the same food.

What the size of the gap does not tell you. It is not a measurement of anybody’s losses. The corrections inside the factors are averages, taken over foods and over people. So the 0.17 is the gap between one measurement and one average. It is not a finding about this food.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke. The figures in this problem are made up.

the calorimeter is worth 10,000 joules for each degree
the thermometer read 21.4 degrees before the sample was lit
the thermometer read 24.9 degrees after the sample had burned
10,000 times 24.9 = 249,000
so the sample released 249,000 joules, which is 249 kilojoules
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the fourth. The energy equivalent converts a rise, and 24.9 is not a rise. It is a reading.

Get the rise first, by taking one reading from the other.

24.9 minus 21.4 = 3.5

Three and a half degrees. Now use the constant on that.

10,000 times 3.5 = 35,000

35,000 divided by 1,000 = 35

Thirty-five kilojoules, not 249.

What went wrong underneath the arithmetic. A Celsius reading is counted from a zero that somebody chose, so the reading itself is not an amount of anything. Only the gap between two readings is. Start the same burn in the same machine from a colder room. You get the same rise and a completely different final reading. The broken method would then give a different energy for the same event.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Every line of the arithmetic is correct. The constant is right and the multiplication is right. And 249 kilojoules is an ordinary size for a food-energy figure, so nothing about the answer looks strange. Only the units catch it: joules for each degree, times degrees, needs a number of degrees, and 24.9 is a position on a scale.

blocks.prompt:
A packet’s nutritional information panel reads: total carbohydrate 30 grams, of which sugars 12 grams; protein 6 grams; total fat 5 grams. The packet is made up for this problem.

Here is a worked answer for the energy in the packet. Find the step that broke.

carbohydrate: 30 times 4 = 120
sugars: 12 times 4 = 48
protein: 6 times 4 = 24
fat: 5 times 9 = 45
120 plus 48 plus 24 plus 45 = 237
so the packet holds 237 kilocalories
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the second. The twelve grams of sugars are not a fourth item. They are part of the thirty grams of carbohydrate, and their energy has already been counted on the line above.

Do it again with three lines instead of four.

30 times 4 = 120

6 times 4 = 24

5 times 9 = 45

120 plus 24 plus 45 = 189

One hundred and eighty-nine kilocalories.

How far out the wrong answer was:

237 minus 189 = 48

48 divided by 189 = 0.253968254

Keep every figure for now, and multiply by a hundred.

0.253968254 times 100 = 25.3968254

Round once, at the end: 25.4. Twenty-five per cent too high, from one extra line.

Why it looks reasonable. Every multiplication is correct and every factor is the right factor. The error is not in the arithmetic at all; it is in reading the panel. A panel nests. The words of which mean the line is a part of the line above it. A part is never added to the whole it came out of.

The habit that catches it. Before you add anything from a panel, check whether the weights you are adding could come to more than the packet does. Thirty plus twelve plus six plus five is fifty-three grams of material. The packet holds thirty grams of carbohydrate in all. The sum has invented twelve grams of food.

blocks.prompt:
A packet in a shop carries this line. The packet and the figure are made up for this problem.

Contains 250 kilocalories.

A colleague reads it and says that eating the packet adds 250 kilocalories to the person who eats it.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute. Two things. First, the same figure in the other unit, so you can see what size of quantity is being talked about. Second, where the 250 came from.

The conversion, using 4.184 kilojoules to the kilocalorie.

250 times 4.184 = 1,046

About a thousand kilojoules.

Where it came from. If the packet is sold in India, the figure was calculated rather than measured. Regulation 5(3)(e)(i) of the labelling regulations of 2020 says the energy to be listed is calculated using conversion factors. So somebody took the grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat, and multiplied each by its factor. Nothing was burned.

Now what the 250 does not establish, which is the part your colleague needs.

It does not establish what the person absorbs. The Atwater factors that produced it carry an average correction for losses in digestion, in absorption and in the urine. An average correction is not this person’s losses on this food. The factors use one value for each of protein, fat and carbohydrate, whatever the food.

It does not establish that the packet holds exactly that. It is arithmetic on declared weights, and the weights are themselves rounded.

It does not establish anything about what the person spends. That is a different quantity entirely and nothing on a packet measures it.

And it does not establish anything about what would change in their body. Going from an intake figure to a change in a body needs one more number. You would need to know what a kilogram of that change is made of. This book does not give you that number, because it depends on what the change is made of. Do not supply it from memory.

The line to say out loud: 250 kilocalories is a property of the packet. It is not an event in a person.

blocks.prompt:
In a district meeting, somebody says this.

Schedule II of the National Food Security Act, 2013 sets the upper primary hot cooked meal at 700 calories. It also sets 20 grams of protein. So every upper primary child gets 700 kilocalories a day from school. We can take that straight off what they need from home.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute. First, read the unit off the Schedule rather than off the sentence. The energy column of Schedule II is headed Calories with Kcal in brackets, so the figure is 700 kilocalories. The speaker said calories and meant kilocalories, and this time they happen to be right.

Second, work out the one thing the two figures in the Schedule can tell you together. That is how much of the energy standard the protein standard accounts for.

20 times 4.0 = 80

80 divided by 700 = 0.1142857143

Keep every figure for now, and turn it into a percentage.

0.1142857143 times 100 = 11.42857143

Round once, at the end: 11.4. About eleven per cent of the energy standard is accounted for by the protein standard. The other eighty-nine per cent has to come from fat and carbohydrate, and Schedule II sets no figure for either. That is worth saying in the meeting, because it is a real gap in what the Schedule fixes.

Now what none of this establishes.

It does not establish that any child received 700 kilocalories. Schedule II is a standard a meal must meet. A standard is a requirement, not a measurement, and the sentence has read one as the other.

It does not establish that a meal that met the standard was eaten, or eaten whole. Nothing in an Act measures a plate.

It does not establish that 700 kilocalories reached a child even if a meal met the standard exactly and was finished. Seven hundred is a food-energy figure. Between the energy in a food and the energy available to the body sit the faecal, gaseous and urinary losses. The figure that reaches the body is always the smaller one.

And the last clause is the one to stop. Taking it straight off what a child needs from home assumes the two flows are independent. It assumes that adding to one leaves the other where it was. The section on stocks and flows says why you cannot assume that. The balance line holds whatever the flows do. It never tells you what happens to one flow when another changes. Whether a school meal displaces food at home is a question about behaviour, and it has to be measured, not assumed.

What to ask for. Weighed portions and plate waste on a sample of days, which turns the Schedule’s requirement into a measurement of what children actually received.
